items.setupText: Choose the words for this introduction.
items.taskText: You meet a new neighbour. Which sentence tells them your job?
options: I am nurse.
I am an nurse.
I am a nurse.
I am the nurse.
items.answer: I am a nurse.
items.explanation: "A nurse" names your job. You are introducing yourself as one member of that profession.

A job such as "nurse" is a singular countable noun. It needs a word such as "a" before it.
"Nurse" begins with the consonant sound /n/, so use "a", not "an".
This introduces your job without assuming that your neighbour already knows about a particular nurse.
This identifies a particular nurse, such as the nurse someone is waiting for. The question asks you to introduce your job.

findings: Photo item repeated the singular-noun frame and gave no reason for individual errors.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite article when naming an occupation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes telling someone a job from identifying a particular worker.
audit.levelReason: A short personal introduction uses an everyday job word and the present form of be.
audit.similarityNote: The only A1 item about an occupation in a first meeting.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: Can I borrow an eraser?
Can I borrow a eraser?
Can I borrow eraser?
Can I borrow an erasers?
items.answer: Can I borrow an eraser?
items.explanation: "Eraser" begins with a vowel sound. For one eraser, say "an eraser".

rationales.Can I borrow an eraser?: "An eraser" correctly asks for one countable object beginning with a vowel sound.
rationales.Can I borrow a eraser?: Use "an" before the vowel sound at the start of "eraser".
rationales.Can I borrow eraser?: "Eraser" names one countable object here, so it cannot stand alone without a determiner.
rationales.Can I borrow an erasers?: "An" is for one object, but "erasers" is plural. Use "an eraser" or simply "erasers".

findings: The original feedback did not explain the vowel sound or singular countability.
audit.microSkill: An before a vowel sound in a request
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the sound of eraser to an and distinguishes singular from plural.
audit.levelReason: A familiar borrowing request contains one concrete object.
audit.similarityNote: Uses a request and contrasts both article choice and noun number.

items.setupText: Choose the words that refer to the door you can both see.
items.taskText: There is just one door in the room. Please close ___ door.
options: a
an
(nothing)
the
items.answer: the
items.explanation: You can both identify the room's one door. "The door" points to that particular door.

rationales.a: "A door" means one door without identifying which. Here the speaker means the room's already identified door.
rationales.an: "Door" starts with /d/, a consonant sound. "An door" is not grammatical.
rationales.(nothing): A singular countable noun such as "door" needs a determiner in this request.
rationales.the: "The" refers to the single door already identified in the room.

findings: The original allowed a possible first-mention reading with A.
audit.microSkill: The for a uniquely identifiable object in the situation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how shared surroundings can make a noun definite without an earlier story about it.
audit.levelReason: The concrete setting and short imperative suit beginning learners.
audit.similarityNote: This is shared physical reference, distinct from later-mention reference.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence about water in general.
items.taskText: Which sentence says what people need every day?
options: People need a water every day.
People need water every day.
People need an water every day.
People need the water every day.
items.answer: People need water every day.
items.explanation: "Water" names a substance in general here. We do not put an article before it: "People need water."

"A water" can mean one serving when ordering a drink. This question is about the substance people need, not a serving.
No article is needed when "water" means the substance in general.
"An" is not used before the consonant sound /w/. It also does not express water as a substance in general.
"The water" refers to particular water already identified. No such water is meant in this general statement.

findings: The old context allowed particular water, and the explanation inserted (nothing) into the sentence.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with a mass noun in a general statement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains why general water differs from a serving or an identified supply.
audit.levelReason: The idea of an everyday need is simple and uses common vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: The set's substance example; other zero-article items have different noun types.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: That is a my coat.
That is the my coat.
That is an my coat.
That is my coat.
items.answer: That is my coat.
items.explanation: "My" already shows whose coat it is. Do not add "a", "an", or "the" before "my".

English does not combine "a" and "my" before the same noun. Say "my coat".
"The" and "my" both identify the noun; they do not go together in "the my coat".
"An" cannot come before the possessive "my". The phrase needs only "my coat".
The possessive "my" supplies the information needed before the singular noun "coat".

findings: Notebook item repeated basic a plus singular noun.
audit.microSkill: No article before a possessive determiner
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents learners from adding an article whenever they see a singular noun.
audit.levelReason: Possession and clothing are familiar A1 language.
audit.similarityNote: Only item testing the interaction of an article with my.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: There is a orange in the bowl.
There is an orange in the bowl.
There is an oranges in the bowl.
There is orange fruit in bowl.
items.answer: There is an orange in the bowl.
items.explanation: "An orange" means one fruit. "Orange" begins with a vowel sound, so the article is "an".

The first sound in "orange" is a vowel; "a orange" should be "an orange".
The article "an" fits both the vowel sound and the singular fruit.
The singular article "an" cannot introduce the plural noun "oranges".
"Bowl" is a singular countable noun and needs a determiner here, for example "in the bowl".

findings: Apple item had generic distractor feedback and repeated a basic noun frame.
audit.microSkill: A countable fruit introduced with there is
audit.pedagogicalValue: Practises an in an existence sentence and keeps singular and plural forms consistent.
audit.levelReason: Food, containers, and there is are early everyday language.
audit.similarityNote: Existence statement about food rather than the request used for eraser.

items.setupText: Choose the word for the same bus.
items.taskText: A bus stops beside us. ___ bus is full.
options: The
A
An
(nothing)
items.answer: The
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces "a bus". The second refers to that same bus, so it says "the bus".

rationales.The: "The bus" takes the reader back to the bus that has just stopped.
rationales.A: "A bus" would introduce a bus without clearly linking it to the one in the first sentence.
rationales.An: "Bus" begins with a consonant sound, so "an bus" is not possible.
rationales.(nothing): "Bus" is singular and countable; it cannot be used without a determiner here.

findings: The old bus outside sentence did not clearly establish the intended reference.
audit.microSkill: A on introduction followed by the for the same referent
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes the change from first to later mention visible across two sentences.
audit.levelReason: Two very short sentences describe a familiar event.
audit.similarityNote: Only A1 item that explicitly links a first and second mention.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence about a general liking.
items.taskText: You like cats of all kinds. What do you say?
options: I like a cats.
I like an cats.
I like cats.
I like the cats.
items.answer: I like cats.
items.explanation: A plural noun with no article can mean the whole kind: "I like cats" means cats in general.

"A" goes with a singular countable noun, not the plural "cats".
"An" cannot introduce a plural noun. It also does not match the initial consonant sound in "cats".
The plural "cats" without an article expresses the general liking described.
This means a particular group of cats that speaker and listener can identify, not cats of all kinds.

findings: The music sentence did not make general versus specific reference explicit.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with generic plural nouns
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts a whole category with a particular identified group.
audit.levelReason: A simple like statement and a familiar plural suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: General plural reference, unlike the uncountable water example.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: We have an small kitchen.
We have a small kitchen.
We have small kitchen.
We have a small kitchens.
items.answer: We have a small kitchen.
items.explanation: Put the article before the adjective: "a small kitchen". "Small" begins with a consonant sound.

Choose the article using the next sound, which is /s/ in "small". It needs "a".
"A" comes before "small" and introduces the one kitchen.
An adjective does not remove the need for an article before the singular noun "kitchen".
"A" introduces one kitchen; "kitchens" is plural and cannot follow it.

findings: Key-on-floor item added no distinction beyond first-mention a.
audit.microSkill: Article before an adjective and a singular noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows the position of the article in a longer noun phrase.
audit.levelReason: Describing a home with one adjective is an A1 task.
audit.similarityNote: The only home-description item with article-adjective-noun order.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: Would you like a apple juice?
Would you like an glass of juice?
Would you like glass of juice?
Would you like a glass of juice?
items.answer: Would you like a glass of juice?
items.explanation: The article belongs to "glass", a countable container. We can offer "a glass of juice" even though juice itself is not counted here.

rationales.Would you like a apple juice?: "Apple" starts with a vowel sound, so an order for one serving would use "an apple juice", not "a apple juice".
rationales.Would you like an glass of juice?: "Glass" begins with /g/, so it takes "a", not "an".
rationales.Would you like glass of juice?: One countable container needs a determiner: "a glass of juice".
rationales.Would you like a glass of juice?: "A" correctly introduces the container "glass"; no second article is needed before "juice".

findings: Umbrella item repeated the simple an-plus-object decision.
audit.microSkill: Article with a container phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Gives learners a practical way to count a drink by its container.
audit.levelReason: Offering a drink is an everyday beginner interaction.
audit.similarityNote: Adds a measure phrase instead of another isolated object.

items.setupText: Choose the word for the marked item.
items.taskText: There are three cups. Only one is blue. Please use ___ blue cup.
options: an
(nothing)
the
a
items.answer: the
items.explanation: The colour identifies one cup among the three. "The blue cup" tells the listener exactly which cup to use.

rationales.an: "Blue" starts with a consonant sound, so "an blue cup" is not grammatical.
rationales.(nothing): The singular noun "cup" still needs a determiner even when an adjective comes before it.
rationales.the: There is exactly one blue cup, so "the" identifies it among the three cups.
rationales.a: "A blue cup" does not mark the already identified unique blue cup as clearly as the definite phrase requested.

findings: Pencil-on-desk item relied on unstated shared knowledge.
audit.microSkill: The when an adjective identifies one member of a group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a description can identify a particular object.
audit.levelReason: Numbers, colours, and a short request are accessible at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Contrast within a visible group differs from the single-door situation.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: We eat breakfast at seven.
We eat a breakfast at a seven.
We eat an breakfast at seven.
We eat breakfast at the seven.
items.answer: We eat breakfast at seven.
items.explanation: The ordinary meal name needs no article in "eat breakfast". A clock time is also used without an article: "at seven".

This uses the usual article-free meal name and clock time.
"A breakfast" can describe one meal, but "at a seven" is not how English gives this clock time.
"An" does not fit the consonant sound /b/. The usual routine expression is simply "eat breakfast".
Do not put "the" before a bare clock time. Say "at seven".

findings: Rice item duplicated a mass-noun choice and showed incorrect capitalisation in alternatives.
audit.microSkill: Zero article in a routine meal and time expression
audit.pedagogicalValue: Builds a complete usable sentence for describing a daily routine.
audit.levelReason: Breakfast and simple clock times belong to everyday beginner language.
audit.similarityNote: Uses a routine expression rather than a general noun category.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the price.
items.taskText: The label says, "Two euros a kilo." What does "a kilo" mean here?
options: For each apple
For each kilo
For half a kilo
For all the apples
items.answer: For each kilo
items.explanation: In this price, "a kilo" means "for each kilo". One kilo costs two euros; two kilos cost four euros.

rationales.For each apple: The unit named is kilo, a weight, not an individual apple.
rationales.For each kilo: Here a means for each unit, and the stated unit is one kilo.
rationales.For half a kilo: The label gives the price for a full kilo. Half a kilo would cost one euro at this rate.
rationales.For all the apples: The price applies to each kilo, not to the whole supply of apples.

findings: Picture-of-house item repeated singular object introduction.
audit.microSkill: Interpreting a as per in a shop price
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the article with the price paid for each unit of weight.
audit.levelReason: A short price calculation and familiar shopping language support A1 comprehension.
audit.similarityNote: The only rate interpretation, using a price label rather than a sentence correction.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: This is a old photo of me.
This is an old photo of me.
This is old photo of me.
This is an old photos of me.
items.answer: This is an old photo of me.
items.explanation: Although "photo" starts with a consonant, the word directly after the article is "old". Its vowel sound requires "an".

Use the first sound of "old", not the first sound of "photo", to choose the article.
"An" correctly comes before the vowel sound in "old" and introduces one photo.
"Old" describes the photo but cannot replace the article needed with this singular noun.
"An" is singular; it cannot be followed by the plural noun "photos".

findings: Elephant item offered another unvaried vowel-initial noun.
audit.microSkill: Article sound determined by an intervening adjective
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents choosing a solely from the sound of the main noun.
audit.levelReason: An old photograph is concrete and the sentence structure is short.
audit.similarityNote: Contrasts adjective sound with noun sound, extending the small-kitchen example.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: Sun is very bright today.
An sun is very bright today.
The sun is very bright today.
The a sun is very bright today.
items.answer: The sun is very bright today.
items.explanation: When we talk about the sun in our sky, we normally say "the sun" because we can identify which sun we mean.

In an ordinary full sentence about our sky, the noun phrase is "the sun", with an article.
"Sun" starts with /s/, so "an sun" is not grammatical.
"The sun" is the usual way to name the familiar sun in our sky.
Do not put "the" and "a" together before the same noun.

findings: Window-near-person item repeated a locative identification frame.
audit.microSkill: The with the familiar sun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Introduces a common definite phrase based on shared world knowledge.
audit.levelReason: Weather and the sky provide familiar concrete vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Shared world knowledge, not a room object or previous sentence, establishes reference.

items.setupText: Choose the usual sentence for saying where you live.
items.taskText: Which sentence uses the city name correctly?
options: I live in a Tokyo.
I live in the Tokyo.
I live in an Tokyo.
I live in Tokyo.
items.answer: I live in Tokyo.
items.explanation: The city name "Tokyo" normally stands alone. Do not add an article when you simply say where you live.

"A Tokyo" is not the usual name of this city in a simple address statement.
The city name does not normally take "the" on its own. Say "in Tokyo".
"An" does not belong before this city name and does not match its initial consonant sound.
The proper name "Tokyo" identifies the city without an article.

findings: Generic books item repeated plural-reference practice and used distracting capitalised options.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with an unmodified city name
audit.pedagogicalValue: Gives a reliable pattern for a common personal-information sentence.
audit.levelReason: Saying where one lives is a central A1 interaction.
audit.similarityNote: Only geographic proper-name item at A1.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have a brother and two sisters.
I have brother and two sisters.
I have an brother and two sisters.
I have a brother and a two sisters.
items.answer: I have a brother and two sisters.
items.explanation: One brother needs "a brother". The number "two" already tells us how many sisters, so no article goes before it here.

This uses "a" for one brother and a number without an article for the sisters.
The singular countable noun "brother" needs a determiner such as "a".
"Brother" begins with the consonant sound /b/, so use "a".
The singular article "a" cannot introduce the plural number phrase "two sisters".

findings: Sandwich item repeated a plus single object without a new contrast.
audit.microSkill: A for one family member versus a number for plural members
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts two noun phrases learners often use in the same introduction.
audit.levelReason: Family descriptions and small numbers fit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Only coordinated singular-and-numbered-plural noun contrast.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: My name is an Ana.
My name is Ana.
My an name is Ana.
An my name is Ana.
items.answer: My name is Ana.
items.explanation: Use a person's ordinary name without an article: "My name is Ana." A vowel at the start of a name does not mean it needs "an".

In a simple self-introduction, the name "Ana" is used without "an".
The personal name identifies the person directly and takes no article in this introduction.
Do not add "an" between the possessive "my" and the noun "name".
An article cannot precede the phrase "my name" in this sentence.

findings: ID-card initialism increased sound complexity while repeating the same vowel-article rule.
audit.microSkill: No article in an ordinary personal-name introduction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Stops learners from applying the a/an sound rule to nouns that need no article.
audit.levelReason: A simple statement of one's name is appropriate for beginners.
audit.similarityNote: Personal naming contrasts with the city name and the occupation introduction.

items.setupText: Choose the word used with this position.
items.taskText: Our lesson is on ___ first floor, not the second floor.
options: a
an
the
(nothing)
items.answer: the
items.explanation: Use "the" with the numbered position "first" here: "the first floor", just as we say "the second floor".

rationales.a: "A first floor" can introduce one in a different description, but this sentence identifies the floor by its position in this building.
rationales.an: "First" begins with a consonant sound, so "an first floor" is not grammatical.
rationales.the: "The first floor" identifies a specific floor by its position.
rationales.(nothing): In this ordinary sentence, the position phrase is "on the first floor", with "the".

findings: Clock-above-board item repeated location-based the.
audit.microSkill: The with first in a building location
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a practical definite phrase for finding a room.
audit.levelReason: First and second with a short location statement are beginner-level language.
audit.similarityNote: Ordinal identification adds a different basis for definiteness.

items.setupText: Choose the usual sentence about speaking a language.
items.taskText: Which sentence names the language correctly?
options: We speak English at home.
We speak an English at home.
We speak a English at home.
We speak the English at home.
items.answer: We speak English at home.
items.explanation: Use the language name on its own in "speak English". An article is not needed to name the language you speak.

"English" names the language directly, without an article.
Although "English" begins with a vowel sound, a language name does not take "an" in this ordinary statement.
"A English" is not the phrase for naming the language. Use "speak English".
"The English" can refer to English people, but the ordinary language phrase here is simply "English".

findings: Tea item allowed a serving interpretation and repeated the mass-noun decision.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with a language name after speak
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates language names from countable things and named groups of people.
audit.levelReason: Talking about languages spoken at home is accessible personal information.
audit.similarityNote: Language reference differs from city and personal names and from general substances.

items.setupText: Choose the words that keep talking about the same car.
items.taskText: I bought a used car yesterday. ___ car needs two new tyres.
options: An
The
A
(nothing)
items.answer: The
items.explanation: "The car" refers back to the used car just introduced. Repeating "a car" would not clearly maintain that reference.

rationales.An: "Car" begins with /k/, so "an car" is incorrect.
rationales.The: The reader already knows which car is being discussed: the one bought yesterday.
rationales.A: This would introduce a car without explicitly linking it to the previous sentence. The task asks you to maintain the same reference.
rationales.(nothing): The singular noun "car" needs a determiner; it cannot start this sentence alone.

findings: Wrong-answer messages did not explain reference or countability.
audit.microSkill: Maintaining a referent across a short narrative
audit.pedagogicalValue: Links the choice of the to continuity in a story.
audit.levelReason: Two past/present sentences describe an everyday purchase and repair.
audit.similarityNote: The A2 set's narrative reference item.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: My new position begins tomorrow. The company has sent me ___ about my first day.
options: an information
a piece of information
an piece of information
a piece of informations
items.answer: a piece of information
items.explanation: "Information" is uncountable. To refer to one detail, use the countable phrase "a piece of information".

rationales.an information: English does not normally count information as "an information". Count a piece or an item of information instead.
rationales.a piece of information: "A" introduces the singular countable noun "piece", while "information" stays uncountable.
rationales.an piece of information: "Piece" starts with /p/, so the article must be "a".
rationales.a piece of informations: The uncountable noun stays "information" after "a piece of"; it does not take plural -s.

findings: Email item repeated a basic sound rule without an A2 distinction.
audit.microSkill: Article with a unit of an uncountable noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches how to count a detail without inventing an information.
audit.levelReason: A workplace message supplies accessible context for a common A2 countability difficulty.
audit.similarityNote: Only item using a piece of with an abstract uncountable noun.

items.setupText: Choose the correct phrase for this feeling.
items.taskText: Please turn the music down. I've got ___ .
options: headache
an headache
a headache
a headaches
items.answer: a headache
items.explanation: The usual expression is "have a headache". "Headache" is a singular countable noun and begins with a pronounced /h/.

rationales.headache: This expression normally needs an article: "I've got a headache".
rationales.an headache: The /h/ in "headache" is pronounced, so use "a".
rationales.a headache: "A headache" correctly names one instance of this discomfort.
rationales.a headaches: "A" cannot introduce the plural "headaches". Use singular "headache" here.

findings: New-tutor item merely retested a before a consonant.
audit.microSkill: A in the fixed expression have a headache
audit.pedagogicalValue: Provides a usable expression for explaining discomfort.
audit.levelReason: Everyday health vocabulary and a simple request fit A2.
audit.similarityNote: The only minor-health expression in the article set.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence about a regular weekly class.
items.taskText: Which sentence uses the day name correctly?
options: We have training every the Monday.
We have training on a Mondays.
We have training on an Mondays.
We have training on Mondays.
items.answer: We have training on Mondays.
items.explanation: "On Mondays" means regularly on that day of the week. The plural day name does not take an article in this expression.

Do not combine "every" with "the" here. You can say "every Monday".
The singular article "a" cannot introduce the plural day name "Mondays".
"An" is singular and does not match either the plural form or the initial consonant sound.
The plural day name without an article expresses the repeated weekly event.

findings: Original Training starts at nine also allowed The training and had a capitalisation cue.
audit.microSkill: No article with plural weekday names for routines
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a regular weekly schedule from an identified individual date.
audit.levelReason: Talking about a weekly class is a routine A2 task.
audit.similarityNote: Time reference adds a new zero-article use.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The college accepts students from many countries. It is ___ .
options: an university
a university
university
a universities
items.answer: a university
items.explanation: "University" starts with the consonant sound /y/, as in "you". The spelling starts with u, but the sound requires "a".

rationales.an university: The initial sound is /y/, not a vowel sound. Write "a university".
rationales.a university: "A" agrees with the initial sound and introduces one institution of this kind.
rationales.university: When classifying this institution after "It is", the singular noun needs a determiner.
rationales.a universities: "A" means one; it cannot be followed by the plural "universities".

findings: Application item retested a simple vowel spelling at too low a demand.
audit.microSkill: A before a written vowel with a consonant sound
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates article choice from the first written letter.
audit.levelReason: A common education word introduces a manageable A2 sound-spelling exception.
audit.similarityNote: Contrasts with the silent-h item rather than repeating it.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that names one hotel of this kind.
items.taskText: We have not chosen where to stay yet. We're looking for ___ near the beach.
options: an small hotel
small hotel
a small hotel
a small hotels
items.answer: a small hotel
items.explanation: "A small hotel" describes the kind of place wanted, without identifying one hotel already chosen. The article comes before "small".

rationales.an small hotel: The first sound after the article is /s/ in "small", so "an" is incorrect.
rationales.small hotel: The singular countable noun "hotel" needs a determiner even when described by "small".
rationales.a small hotel: This describes an as-yet-unidentified member of the category the travellers want.
rationales.a small hotels: The singular article "a" cannot go with plural "hotels".

findings: Original repeated the same two-sentence later-mention car pattern.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite reference to something sought but not yet selected
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that a can introduce a desired object without asserting a known example.
audit.levelReason: Accommodation search and a short adjective phrase suit A2.
audit.similarityNote: A future choice of accommodation rather than reference to an existing possession.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: Flights are expensive, so we're going to Paris ___ .
options: by train
by a train
by an train
by the train
items.answer: by train
items.explanation: Use "by train" to name the means of travel. In this expression, "by" is followed by the transport word without an article.

rationales.by train: This names the method of travel using the standard "by + transport" expression.
rationales.by a train: For the travel method, say "by train". To name a vehicle, use a different construction such as "on a train".
rationales.by an train: "An" does not fit /t/, and the transport expression needs no article.
rationales.by the train: "By the train" can mean beside a train, but it does not express the intended travel method here.

findings: Passport sentence added no article contrast beyond singular a.
audit.microSkill: Zero article when naming a transport method with by
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes travelling by train from being beside a particular train.
audit.levelReason: Planning travel is a common A2 situation.
audit.similarityNote: Only transport-method article item at A2.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The repair took exactly sixty minutes: ___ .
options: a hour
an hour
an hours
hour
items.answer: an hour
items.explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because its h is silent. One period of sixty minutes is "an hour".

rationales.a hour: The first spoken sound in "hour" is a vowel, so "a" must become "an".
rationales.an hour: The article follows the sound, not the silent written h.
rationales.hour: To name one countable period here, include the article: "an hour".

findings: The original did not explain the silent h.
audit.microSkill: An before silent h in hour
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes pronunciation the basis of the article decision.
audit.levelReason: A common duration word supplies an accessible A2 exception.
audit.similarityNote: Silent consonant contrasts with the pronounced initial sound in university.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for all the details printed on this ticket.
items.taskText: Check ___ before you travel.
options: an information on your ticket
a information on your ticket
the information on your ticket
the informations on your ticket
items.answer: the information on your ticket
items.explanation: "On your ticket" identifies the information to check. Although "information" is uncountable, it can take "the" when it refers to specific details.

rationales.an information on your ticket: "Information" is uncountable; "an information" is not a standard singular unit.
rationales.a information on your ticket: The uncountable noun does not take "a", and the following sound is a vowel as well.
rationales.the information on your ticket: "The" identifies the particular set of details printed on the ticket.
rationales.the informations on your ticket: "Information" does not normally have a plural -s form in English.

findings: Original feedback did not teach that uncountable nouns can take the.
audit.microSkill: The with identified uncountable information
audit.pedagogicalValue: Counters the mistaken rule that uncountable nouns never take an article.
audit.levelReason: Checking a ticket gives the added phrase a clear everyday function.
audit.similarityNote: Specific mass reference contrasts with the separate unit-of-information item.

items.setupText: Choose the words for this country name.
items.taskText: My sister lives in ___ United States.
options: a
an
(nothing)
the
items.answer: the
items.explanation: The conventional country name is "the United States". Some multiword country names use "the", even though names such as Japan do not.

rationales.a: "A United States" does not name the country in this ordinary location sentence.
rationales.an: The name does not take "an"; "United" also starts with a consonant sound.
rationales.(nothing): The country name normally includes "the" in a full sentence: "in the United States".
rationales.the: "The United States" is the established form of this country name.

findings: Patience sentence repeated generic uncountable reference without contrasting noun types.
audit.microSkill: The in the established name the United States
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows why learners must learn articles as part of some place names.
audit.levelReason: A common country name and family location are suitable A2 content.
audit.similarityNote: The set's country-name exception.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The map has bus routes and opening times. What ___ !
options: an useful guide
useful guide
a useful guide
a useful guides
items.answer: a useful guide
items.explanation: The exclamation is "What a useful guide!". "Useful" begins with the consonant sound /y/, so it takes "a".

rationales.an useful guide: The written u in "useful" represents a /y/ sound at the start. Use "a".
rationales.useful guide: A singular countable noun in this exclamation needs an article: "What a useful guide!".
rationales.a useful guide: This puts "a" before the adjective and uses the correct sound-based choice.
rationales.a useful guides: "A" cannot introduce the plural "guides" in this exclamation.

findings: The useful-map sentence lacked an explanation of the sound-spelling contrast.
audit.microSkill: Article in a what exclamation with a singular noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a common positive response as a complete phrase.
audit.levelReason: Short exclamations with familiar adjectives extend A2 conversational range.
audit.similarityNote: Exclamation structure differs from the university classification item.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: At the cafe: "Two coffees, please: ___ and a cappuccino."
options: a espresso
an espresso
an espressos
a espressos
items.answer: an espresso
items.explanation: A drink name can be countable when it means one serving. "An espresso" is one serving, and "espresso" begins with a vowel sound.

rationales.a espresso: For this vowel sound, the singular article is "an".
rationales.an espresso: This correctly names one serving of espresso within the two-drink order.
rationales.a espressos: "A" cannot introduce plural "espressos" and does not match the initial vowel sound.

findings: Umbrella item repeated object counting and did not extend A2 control.
audit.microSkill: An with a drink interpreted as one serving
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that context can make a normally uncountable drink countable.
audit.levelReason: Ordering two drinks is practical A2 language.
audit.similarityNote: Serving interpretation contrasts with abstract information and countable containers.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: Both bags look blue to me. Are they ___ colour?
options: a same
an same
same
the same
items.answer: the same
items.explanation: The normal expression is "the same colour". English uses "the" with "same" in this comparison.

rationales.a same: Do not use "a same" in this expression; say "the same".
rationales.an same: "An same" is not the expression and also mismatches the /s/ sound.
rationales.same: In this full question, include "the": "Are they the same colour?".
rationales.the same: "The same colour" asks whether the colours match.

findings: Printer-by-door item did not rule out another indefinite reading.
audit.microSkill: The in the expression the same
audit.pedagogicalValue: Supplies an article pattern that transfers to the same size, price, and time.
audit.levelReason: Comparing the colours of two objects suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Fixed comparison expression rather than identifying an object by location.

items.setupText: Choose the ordinary way to name the sport.
items.taskText: After work, we usually play ___ with our neighbours.
options: tennis
a tennis
an tennis
the tennis
items.answer: tennis
items.explanation: Sport names normally have no article after "play": "play tennis". The sentence names an activity, not one countable match.

rationales.tennis: "Play tennis" is the standard phrase for taking part in this sport.
rationales.a tennis: "Tennis" does not count a single match. You could say "a game of tennis".
rationales.an tennis: "An" neither fits the initial consonant sound nor belongs before this sport name here.
rationales.the tennis: The usual activity phrase is "play tennis". "The tennis" can refer to a particular competition in other constructions.

findings: Original study English item repeated a beginner language-name rule.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with a sport after play
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches an activity expression and distinguishes it from a countable game.
audit.levelReason: Leisure activities and frequency are established A2 contexts.
audit.similarityNote: Only sporting activity in the A2 set.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: We usually eat toast, but yesterday the hotel served us ___ .
options: an big breakfast
big breakfast
a big breakfast
a big breakfasts
items.answer: a big breakfast
items.explanation: An ordinary meal name can become countable when we describe one particular meal: "a big breakfast".

rationales.an big breakfast: "Big" begins with /b/, so the article is "a".
rationales.big breakfast: The phrase describes one meal with an adjective; it needs a determiner such as "a" here.
rationales.a big breakfast: "A" introduces one breakfast described as big, rather than the routine activity of eating breakfast.
rationales.a big breakfasts: "A" introduces one meal and cannot be followed by plural "breakfasts".

findings: Receipt item repeated indefinite singular counting.
audit.microSkill: A with a described instance of a meal
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends the familiar article-free meal expression to one described meal.
audit.levelReason: A hotel breakfast is a concrete A2 narrative context.
audit.similarityNote: Meal reinterpretation differs from counting a cafe drink.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: At reception, please show ___ with a photo.
options: a ID card
an ID card
an ID cards
ID card
items.answer: an ID card
items.explanation: The letter I is pronounced with a vowel sound. Because ID is read as letter names, the phrase is "an ID card".

rationales.a ID card: Use the sound of the letter name I. It begins with a vowel sound and needs "an".
rationales.an ID card: "An" matches the spoken beginning of ID and introduces one card.
rationales.an ID cards: The article is singular, so the noun must be "card", not "cards".
rationales.ID card: The singular countable phrase needs a determiner in this request.

findings: Online-course item offered another uncomplicated vowel-initial noun phrase.
audit.microSkill: An before an initialism pronounced with a vowel sound
audit.pedagogicalValue: Transfers the sound rule to letters read aloud.
audit.levelReason: Showing identification is a common adult A2 transaction.
audit.similarityNote: An initialism adds a distinct sound decision beyond hour and useful.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: Our new flat is farther from the station, but it is ___ of the three we saw.
options: a cheapest
an cheapest
cheapest
the cheapest
items.answer: the cheapest
items.explanation: "The cheapest" identifies the flat with the lowest price in the stated group of three. This superlative takes "the".

rationales.a cheapest: The phrase identifies the lowest-priced member of a defined group, so use "the cheapest".
rationales.an cheapest: "An" does not fit the consonant sound and is not the article for this identifying superlative.
rationales.cheapest: Include "the" before this superlative when identifying one flat among the three.
rationales.the cheapest: "The" works with the superlative to identify the lowest-priced flat in the comparison.

findings: Address-on-form item repeated location-based definite reference.
audit.microSkill: The with an identifying superlative
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a superlative selects a member of a stated comparison group.
audit.levelReason: Housing prices and common superlatives are suitable A2 language.
audit.similarityNote: The set's ranked comparison, distinct from the same colour.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: My brother gave me some useful advice.
My brother gave me an useful advice.
My brother gave me a useful advice.
My brother gave me some useful advices.
items.answer: My brother gave me some useful advice.
items.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so "some useful advice" works without a or an. An adjective does not make advice countable.

"Some" can introduce an unspecified amount of the uncountable noun "advice".
"Advice" cannot be introduced by "an" here, and "useful" begins with a consonant sound.
An adjective does not turn "advice" into a singular countable noun. Say "some useful advice" or "a useful piece of advice".
The noun remains "advice", without plural -s, in standard English.

findings: Original advice blank could allow the advice and did not explain countability.
audit.microSkill: Some rather than a or an with modified advice
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the effect of adding an adjective to an uncountable noun.
audit.levelReason: Giving and receiving advice in family contexts fits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Quantified abstract noun complements the definite-information example.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: I take this medicine twice ___ : once in the morning and once at night.
options: an day
a day
a days
day
items.answer: a day
items.explanation: "Twice a day" means two times each day. Here "a" expresses a repeated rate, not an unidentified calendar day.

rationales.an day: "Day" begins with /d/, so it cannot follow "an".
rationales.a day: "A day" expresses the daily frequency and matches the two times specified.
rationales.a days: The article "a" takes the singular unit "day", not plural "days".
rationales.day: The frequency expression requires "a day" or "per day" after "twice".

findings: Short-answer item repeated a plus adjective without a new usage.
audit.microSkill: A expressing frequency per unit of time
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects an article pattern with understanding a routine instruction.
audit.levelReason: Frequency and daily routines are A2 language; no medical decision is tested.
audit.similarityNote: Temporal rate differs from singular objects and identified times.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The shop assistant offers two sizes: "Would you like ___ ?"
options: small or large bag
an small or an large bag
a small or a large bag
a small or a large bags
items.answer: a small or a large bag
items.explanation: Each size describes a possible singular bag. The phrase "a small or a large bag" uses an article before each alternative.

rationales.small or large bag: The singular noun "bag" needs a determiner in this full question, even when two adjectives are offered.
rationales.an small or an large bag: Both "small" and "large" begin with consonant sounds, so neither can follow "an".
rationales.a small or a large bag: Both alternatives correctly introduce a possible singular bag with "a".
rationales.a small or a large bags: The article "a" cannot introduce the plural noun "bags".

findings: Account item supplied another isolated an answer with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Articles in coordinated alternatives sharing a noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how to offer alternatives while keeping singular articles consistent.
audit.levelReason: Choosing a bag size is a concrete transactional task at A2.
audit.similarityNote: The only either-size alternative construction in this set.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for the general activity.
items.taskText: Daria works in a bookshop and enjoys ___ about books with customers.
options: a conversation
conversation
an conversation
a conversations
items.answer: conversation
items.explanation: Here "conversation" names the activity of talking in general, so no article is needed. "A conversation" would count one particular exchange.

rationales.a conversation: This would count a single exchange. The task asks for the general activity she enjoys as part of her work.
rationales.conversation: The uncountable use names the activity without counting individual exchanges.
rationales.an conversation: "Conversation" begins with /k/, so "an" is not possible.
rationales.a conversations: The singular article cannot introduce the plural form "conversations".

findings: Original generic Reports sentence did not distinguish general from identified reports.
audit.microSkill: Activity reading versus one instance of conversation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that the same noun may name an activity or a countable event.
audit.levelReason: A familiar work routine supports a B1 shift between countable and uncountable meaning.
audit.similarityNote: Only general conversation activity in the set.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The old recipe is difficult to follow. Could you give me ___ of how to make the sauce?
options: an clearer explanation
clearer explanation
a clearer explanation
a clearer explanations
items.answer: a clearer explanation
items.explanation: "Explanation" is countable here. The comparative adjective stays inside the noun phrase: "a clearer explanation".

rationales.an clearer explanation: The next sound is /k/ in "clearer", so the article must be "a".
rationales.clearer explanation: The adjective does not supply the determiner needed with singular countable "explanation".
rationales.a clearer explanation: This correctly asks for one explanation that is clearer than the current one.
rationales.a clearer explanations: "A" requires a singular noun, so plural "explanations" cannot follow.

findings: Original useful-explanation item repeated A2 sound selection with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Article with a comparative adjective and countable abstract noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves article use when a learner expands an abstract noun phrase.
audit.levelReason: A request for clarification and comparative description are appropriate B1 functions.
audit.similarityNote: A comparative request in cooking, unlike the narrative and institutional items.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for a second, different message.
items.taskText: I sent one email this morning. Now I need to send ___ with the missing attachment.
options: a other email
an other email
another email
another an email
items.answer: another email
items.explanation: "Another" means one more or a different one. It already contains the indefinite idea, so say "another email" without adding a or an.

rationales.a other email: The standard single word is "another", not the separate phrase "a other".
rationales.an other email: In this ordinary use, "another" is written as one word.
rationales.another email: This correctly introduces a further email distinct from the first.
rationales.another an email: Do not add a second indefinite article after "another".

findings: Original email sentence was another elementary an-before-vowel item.
audit.microSkill: Another introducing an additional singular item
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents double articles and links a determiner to sequence of communication.
audit.levelReason: Correcting an everyday message is a practical B1 context.
audit.similarityNote: Only additional-item use of another.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for the roof belonging to the rented house.
items.taskText: We rented a house beside the lake, but ___ leaks whenever it rains.
options: the roof
an roof
roof
these roof
items.answer: the roof
items.explanation: The house has introduced an associated roof even though the word "roof" is new. "The roof" means the roof of that house.

rationales.the roof: The rented house makes its roof identifiable, so the first mention of roof can still use "the".
rationales.an roof: "Roof" starts with a consonant sound, so "an roof" is incorrect.
rationales.roof: A singular countable "roof" needs a determiner in this clause.
rationales.these roof: "These" introduces plural nouns. A single roof would use "this roof" or, for the intended link, "the roof".

findings: Original confidential-information item repeated a postmodifier without teaching reference.
audit.microSkill: The on first mention through a part-whole association
audit.pedagogicalValue: Corrects the mistaken rule that every first mention must use a or an.
audit.levelReason: A concrete house-and-roof relationship supports B1 reference beyond literal repetition.
audit.similarityNote: An associated part rather than the same repeated noun.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The detective cannot solve the case on a guess. She needs ___ .
options: an evidence
a convincing evidence
a pieces of evidence
convincing evidence
items.answer: convincing evidence
items.explanation: "Evidence" is uncountable in this meaning. Say "convincing evidence", or use a unit such as "a piece of evidence".

rationales.an evidence: English does not normally count a clue as "an evidence"; it can be a piece of evidence.
rationales.a convincing evidence: Adding an adjective does not make "evidence" a singular countable noun.
rationales.a pieces of evidence: The article "a" needs singular "piece", not plural "pieces".
rationales.convincing evidence: This correctly uses the uncountable noun without an indefinite article.

findings: The old context allowed the additional evidence and offered only generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Uncountable evidence versus a countable unit
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a common abstract noun that differs in countability across languages.
audit.levelReason: A short detective scenario makes an abstract B1 noun concrete.
audit.similarityNote: Evidence after an adjective, distinct from counting a conversation.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the sentence.
items.taskText: "The students in the evening class asked for a later deadline." Who does "the students" identify?
options: Any students who might attend an evening class in future
The particular group belonging to the evening class being discussed
One representative student from any evening class
Students as a general category, including those in morning classes
items.answer: The particular group belonging to the evening class being discussed
items.explanation: "The" and "in the evening class" identify a particular group. The sentence reports what that group did; it is not a general statement about all students.

rationales.Any students who might attend an evening: The definite group is connected to the class being discussed, and the past-tense request has already happened.
rationales.The particular group belonging to the ev: This preserves the definite plural reference and its identifying modifier.
rationales.One representative student from any even: "Students" is plural and identifies a group, not one representative individual.
rationales.Students as a general category, includin: The phrase restricts reference to the identified evening class.

findings: Original allowed both Students and The students despite marking only zero article correct.
audit.microSkill: Interpreting a definite plural group with a restricting phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the meaning contrast instead of declaring a grammatical alternative wrong.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a defined group in a familiar class situation fits B1.
audit.similarityNote: Only explicit plural-group reference interpretation.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: In the instructions, please include ___ so readers can see exactly what to do.
options: an example
a example
an examples
example
items.answer: an example
items.explanation: A single demonstration is "an example". "Example" is countable and begins with a vowel sound.

rationales.an example: This introduces one illustrative case and uses the correct vowel-based article.
rationales.a example: The first sound in "example" is a vowel, so use "an".
rationales.example: A singular countable example needs a determiner here.

findings: Original explanation did not connect the counted noun to its meaning.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite article introducing an illustrative case
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects an abstract countable noun to a clear communicative purpose.
audit.levelReason: Requesting a clarifying example is useful B1 functional language.
audit.similarityNote: An instruction-writing context introduces an illustration, rather than a physical object.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: It was a honest mistake, not a deliberate lie.
It was an honest mistake, not a deliberate lie.
It was an honest mistake, not an deliberate lie.
It was honest mistake, not deliberate lie.
items.answer: It was an honest mistake, not a deliberate lie.
items.explanation: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound because h is silent; "deliberate" begins with /d/. The contrast therefore needs "an honest mistake" and "a deliberate lie".

rationales.It was a honest mistake, not a deliberat: The silent h in "honest" requires "an", not "a".
rationales.It was an honest mistake, not a delibera: Both articles follow the sounds of their adjectives and introduce singular countable nouns.
rationales.It was an honest mistake, not an deliber: "Deliberate" begins with a consonant sound, so the second article must be "a".
rationales.It was honest mistake, not deliberate li: Both singular countable nouns need determiners in this full sentence.

findings: Original honest-apology item did not explain silent h and lacked a contrast.
audit.microSkill: Contrasting article sounds across two modified abstract nouns
audit.pedagogicalValue: Applies the sound rule twice while distinguishing an accident from deliberate action.
audit.levelReason: A short explanation of responsibility uses accessible B1 concepts.
audit.similarityNote: The only paired sound contrast in a correction of intent.

items.setupText: Choose the expression for the already identified train.
items.taskText: My ticket says 8:15, platform four. I'll meet you on ___ from Brighton.
options: an 8:15 train
8:15 train
these 8:15 train
the 8:15 train
items.answer: the 8:15 train
items.explanation: The departure time identifies the booked service. "The 8:15 train" refers to that particular train, rather than naming travel by train in general.

rationales.an 8:15 train: This can introduce an unspecified service leaving at that time, but the prompt asks for the train already identified by the ticket.
rationales.8:15 train: The singular countable noun phrase needs a determiner here.
rationales.these 8:15 train: "These" is plural, while the ticket identifies one train.
rationales.the 8:15 train: The time and ticket establish the particular service being referenced.

findings: Schedule-on-wall item did not establish a uniquely intended schedule.
audit.microSkill: The for a scheduled service identified by time
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an identified vehicle from an article-free mode of travel.
audit.levelReason: Coordinating travel arrangements is a familiar B1 task.
audit.similarityNote: Timetable-based identification differs from association with a house.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase in standard British English.
items.taskText: Both families need a place to live. The charity helps people find ___ .
options: an accommodation
a suitable accommodation
suitable accommodation
a suitable accommodations
items.answer: suitable accommodation
items.explanation: In the housing sense used here, standard British English treats "accommodation" as uncountable: "suitable accommodation". American English also uses plural "accommodations", but none of the offered indefinite-article forms fits.

rationales.an accommodation: For somewhere to live in this usage, use uncountable "accommodation"; count "a room" or "a flat" instead.
rationales.a suitable accommodation: The housing noun is uncountable in this reading. Other meanings of "an accommodation", such as an adjustment or compromise, are different.
rationales.suitable accommodation: This describes housing without trying to count it as one accommodation.
rationales.a suitable accommodations: The singular article "a" cannot introduce plural "accommodations", even in varieties that use that plural for lodging.

findings: Original discussed housing could also take the housing in a specific reading.
audit.microSkill: Uncountable accommodation in a housing context
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the noun's intended sense and acknowledges the relevant dialect distinction.
audit.levelReason: Finding somewhere to live is practical B1 language with a common countability trap.
audit.similarityNote: Housing vocabulary provides a sense-sensitive countability example.

items.setupText: Choose the words for a new decision, rather than one previously identified.
items.taskText: After considering several options, the team reached ___ about where to hold the event.
options: decision
an decision
a decision
a decisions
items.answer: a decision
items.explanation: "Reach a decision" introduces one outcome of discussion. "Decision" is countable and starts with a consonant sound.

rationales.decision: The singular countable noun needs a determiner: "reach a decision".
rationales.a decision: This introduces a newly reached outcome rather than referring to an already identified decision.
rationales.a decisions: The singular article cannot be used before plural "decisions".

findings: Original feedback did not explain the new countable outcome.
audit.microSkill: A introducing the outcome in reach a decision
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches an article as part of a productive discussion expression.
audit.levelReason: Group planning and reporting an outcome are B1 functions.
audit.similarityNote: An outcome of deliberation differs from an example or explanation.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
items.taskText: "Before the meeting, I read a paper about local water use." What does "a paper" most naturally mean here?
options: Paper as a material for printing
One written article or study
All the documents required for the meeting
A quantity of blank sheets
items.answer: One written article or study
items.explanation: With "a" and a topic introduced by "about", "paper" means a countable piece of writing. Article-free "paper" can name the material instead.

rationales.Paper as a material for printing: The article and the action of reading a work about a subject support the countable written-work meaning.
rationales.One written article or study: The phrase names one work of writing on the specified subject.
rationales.All the documents required for the meeti: "A paper" is singular and does not mean the entire set of documents.
rationales.A quantity of blank sheets: Blank sheets would not be read for information about water use.

findings: Old-invoice item repeated an-before-vowel without a new reading demand.
audit.microSkill: A paper as a written work rather than material
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes an article-dependent change of noun meaning explicit.
audit.levelReason: Reading a short work-related article is a familiar B1 task.
audit.similarityNote: Material-versus-document sense, distinct from abstract activity versus event.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase identifying the remaining key.
items.taskText: There were two keys. I have one; do you have ___ ?
options: another key
the other key
an other key
other key
items.answer: the other key
items.explanation: Only two keys are in the stated set. Once one is identified, "the other key" identifies the single remaining key.

rationales.another key: This asks for an additional key without explicitly marking it as the remaining member of the known pair.
rationales.the other key: The two-key context makes the remaining key uniquely identifiable.
rationales.an other key: The ordinary indefinite form is the single word "another"; it still would not express the definite remaining member as directly.
rationales.other key: The singular countable phrase needs a determiner; for this pair, use "the other key".

findings: Answer-at-bottom item was another weak locative definite cloze.
audit.microSkill: The other for the remaining member of a pair
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts definite remaining reference with indefinite another.
audit.levelReason: A two-item practical situation gives B1 learners a clear determiner contrast.
audit.similarityNote: Paired-item reference complements the additional-email item.

items.setupText: Choose the words for the general field of study.
items.taskText: Her degree is in ___ ; she studies how people use limited resources.
options: an economics
a economics
the economics
economics
items.answer: economics
items.explanation: The name of the field is "economics", without an article in "a degree in economics". Its final -s does not make it a set of countable objects.

rationales.an economics: The field name is not a singular countable item that can be introduced with "an".
rationales.a economics: The ordinary name of the subject takes no indefinite article.
rationales.the economics: "The economics of a project" can refer to a project's financial aspects, but the question names the general field of study.
rationales.economics: The article-free subject name matches the stated degree field.

findings: Reliable-data item provided no clear general-versus-specific constraint.
audit.microSkill: Zero article with a discipline name ending in s
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a field name from both plural count nouns and a specific project's economics.
audit.levelReason: Discussing a degree and its subject fits B1 educational language.
audit.similarityNote: A field-of-study example with a misleading noun ending.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence that describes the ordinary purpose of attending school.
items.taskText: Speaking about his children as pupils, a parent says:
options: They go to school by bus.
They go to a school by a bus.
They go to an school by bus.
They go to school by an bus.
items.answer: They go to school by bus.
items.explanation: "Go to school" uses school for its normal educational activity. "By bus" names a transport method without an article.

Both conventional expressions fit: attending school as pupils and travelling by bus.
"A school" can introduce a particular institution, but "by a bus" is not the intended transport-method expression.
"School" begins with a consonant sound and cannot follow "an".
"An bus" mismatches the initial sound, and the transport expression needs no article.

findings: Broken-printer item repeated simple singular a with no B1 extension.
audit.microSkill: Bare school for its institutional activity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects article omission with a conventional social activity.
audit.levelReason: School attendance and travel routines are accessible B1 content.
audit.similarityNote: Institutional attendance differs from generic fields or particular buildings.

items.setupText: Choose the correct phrase for this building's unique exit of that kind.
items.taskText: The plan shows just one emergency exit. Staff must keep ___ clear.
options: an emergency exits
emergency exit
the emergency exit
these emergency exit
items.answer: the emergency exit
items.explanation: The plan establishes one exit of this kind. "The emergency exit" refers back to that identified exit.

rationales.emergency exit: The singular countable phrase needs a determiner in this instruction.
rationales.the emergency exit: The definite article identifies the exit already established by the plan.

findings: Original emergency-exit item tested only the vowel sound.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference maintained across a safety instruction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a described plan to an instruction about the same identified object.
audit.levelReason: A short workplace safety instruction suits B1 reading.
audit.similarityNote: An identified functional exit rather than an associated part or scheduled vehicle.

items.setupText: Choose the article used in this river name.
items.taskText: Their cycling route follows ___ Thames from Oxford towards London.
options: a
an
the
(nothing)
items.answer: the
items.explanation: The conventional river name is "the Thames". English normally uses "the" with named rivers in full sentences.

rationales.a: "A Thames" does not name the identified river along this route.
rationales.an: The name does not take an indefinite article, and its initial sound is a consonant.
rationales.the: "The Thames" is the established river name in this geographical context.
rationales.(nothing): In an ordinary sentence naming the river, include "the".

findings: Original students-who-missed-test sentence also allowed zero article.
audit.microSkill: The with a named river
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends proper-name article knowledge beyond city and country names.
audit.levelReason: Describing a travel route gives a familiar B1 setting for a geographical convention.
audit.similarityNote: Only river-name article use.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: At the end of each placement, trainees receive ___ about their work.
options: a detailed feedback
detailed feedback
an detailed feedback
detailed feedbacks
items.answer: detailed feedback
items.explanation: "Feedback" is uncountable in this context. Say "detailed feedback", without a or an and without plural -s.

rationales.a detailed feedback: The adjective detailed does not make feedback countable. You can receive "a detailed comment" but not normally "a detailed feedback".
rationales.detailed feedback: This correctly treats the comments as an uncountable body of feedback.
rationales.an detailed feedback: Feedback does not take an indefinite article in this meaning; an also mismatches the /d/ sound in detailed.
rationales.detailed feedbacks: Use the uncountable form feedback. To count individual points, use a plural noun such as comments.

findings: Original request could refer to the feedback and used capitalised distractors inside a sentence.
audit.microSkill: No indefinite article with modified feedback
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an uncountable body of feedback from individual countable comments.
audit.levelReason: A training context uses relevant B1 vocabulary and a simple general statement.
audit.similarityNote: A body of evaluative comments rather than the supporting evidence or available housing used elsewhere.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for an unspecified number of useful summaries.
items.taskText: The librarian found ___ of the debate, so I could compare different accounts.
options: a useful summaries
an useful summaries
some useful summaries
some a useful summaries
items.answer: some useful summaries
items.explanation: "Summaries" is plural. "Some useful summaries" introduces an unspecified number; a and an would require a singular noun.

rationales.an useful summaries: "An" is singular and also does not match the initial consonant sound in "useful".
rationales.some useful summaries: "Some" correctly introduces the unspecified plural accounts needed for comparison.
rationales.some a useful summaries: Do not combine "some" and "a" before this noun phrase; the plural noun also rules out "a".

findings: Original useful-summary item repeated singular a and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite plural some contrasted with a and an
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects article number to a real need for multiple accounts.
audit.levelReason: Comparing short accounts is a manageable B1 reading-related activity.
audit.similarityNote: Only indefinite plural-quantity choice in the set.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that makes the intended contrast.
items.taskText: On most days the room is used as a classroom, but tonight it is ___ for the visiting performers.
options: a rehearsal space
an rehearsal space
rehearsal space a
a rehearsal spaces
items.answer: a rehearsal space
items.explanation: Here "space" means one area serving a particular purpose, so "a rehearsal space" is countable. In "We need more space", it would instead mean uncountable available room.

rationales.a rehearsal space: This classifies the room as one area used for rehearsals tonight.
rationales.an rehearsal space: The next sound is /r/ in "rehearsal", so the article must be "a".
rationales.rehearsal space a: An article comes before the noun phrase, not after it.
rationales.a rehearsal spaces: The singular article cannot introduce plural "spaces".

findings: Original unusual-error item was a repeated basic an choice.
audit.microSkill: Countable space for an area assigned a purpose
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how meaning changes the countability and article pattern of space.
audit.levelReason: Temporary room use is concrete enough for B1 count/mass comparison.
audit.similarityNote: Physical area versus available room, distinct from document and activity senses.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
items.taskText: "It was a most enjoyable evening." What does "a most enjoyable evening" mean here?
options: The most enjoyable evening out of every evening compared
A very enjoyable evening, without an explicit ranking
An evening enjoyed by most of the guests
An evening that was enjoyable for most of its duration
items.answer: A very enjoyable evening, without an explicit ranking
items.explanation: In this formal expression, "a most enjoyable" means "a very enjoyable". "The most enjoyable" would identify the top evening in a comparison.

rationales.The most enjoyable evening out of every: That is the normal ranking meaning of "the most enjoyable evening", not the intensifying use with "a".
rationales.A very enjoyable evening, without an exp: The indefinite article supports the formal intensifier meaning of most.
rationales.An evening enjoyed by most of the guests: "Most" modifies enjoyable here; it does not count the guests.
rationales.An evening that was enjoyable for most o: Nothing in the article phrase divides the evening into enjoyable and unenjoyable periods.

findings: Original most-useful-form item tested a basic superlative article only.
audit.microSkill: A most as an intensifier versus the most as a ranking
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that apparently similar article phrases can perform different evaluations.
audit.levelReason: The less common formal intensifier and its distinction from a familiar superlative suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Only intensifying most construction.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation that preserves the writer's emphasis.
items.taskText: "We still have a few seats, so you can join us." Why does "a few" fit the invitation?
options: It presents the small number of remaining seats positively as available
It emphasises that almost no seats remain and therefore discourages attendance
It identifies seats already reserved for the listener
It says the speaker cannot estimate whether any seats remain
items.answer: It presents the small number of remaining seats positively as available
items.explanation: "A few" means some, though not many. That positive orientation supports "you can join us". Bare "few" would emphasise scarcity instead.

rationales.It presents the small number of remainin: The article changes the orientation towards the seats that do remain, which supports the invitation.
rationales.It emphasises that almost no seats remai: That interpretation is closer to bare "few" and conflicts with the invitation.
rationales.It identifies seats already reserved for: "A few" indicates an unspecified number; it does not identify reserved seats.
rationales.It says the speaker cannot estimate whet: The phrase asserts that some seats remain, though it does not give an exact count.

findings: Original unusually-careful item tested only an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: Positive orientation created by a in a few
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the small article to the practical implication of an invitation.
audit.levelReason: B2 interpretation goes beyond quantity to the speaker's argumentative emphasis.
audit.similarityNote: Countable quantity orientation, paired conceptually but not structurally with little.

items.setupText: Choose the wording that supports the stated reason for cancelling.
items.taskText: The guide cancels the climb because the group has almost no experience. Which explanation keeps that emphasis?
options: We have a little experience of climbing.
We have little experience of climbing.
We have a little of the experience of climbing.
We have the little experience of climbing.
items.answer: We have little experience of climbing.
items.explanation: Bare "little" stresses how limited the experience is. "A little" stresses the existence of some experience, which would support a more positive argument.

This highlights the experience the group does have. It does not preserve the requested emphasis on near-absence.
Bare little gives the negative orientation needed to explain the cancellation.
rationales.We have a little of the experience of cl: This awkwardly treats the experience as an identified whole with a small portion; that is not the general lack described.
rationales.We have the little experience of climbin: "The little experience" normally needs a defining continuation such as "we gained last year". It does not express the intended general shortfall here.

findings: Original clearer-policy item used formal content for an elementary a decision.
audit.microSkill: Bare little versus a little in an explanatory argument
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how article choice affects whether a quantity supports or undermines a conclusion.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting the reason for a decision through quantity orientation suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: A negative uncountable evaluation, distinct from the positive invitation with seats.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the first phrase.
items.taskText: "The form was confusing by design, not by accident." What does "by design" mean?
options: According to the particular drawing already mentioned
Intentionally, as part of how it was planned
Through the work of the design department alone
Because the completed design was physically beside the form
items.answer: Intentionally, as part of how it was planned
items.explanation: Article-free "by design" is a fixed expression meaning intentionally. It is not a reference to one drawing or one named department.

rationales.According to the particular drawing alre: That would treat design as an identified document; the article-free expression instead expresses intention.
rationales.Intentionally, as part of how it was pla: The contrast with "by accident" confirms the intentional meaning.
rationales.Through the work of the design departmen: The phrase describes intention, not which department is responsible.
rationales.Because the completed design was physica: Although by can mean beside, the parallel with "by accident" rules out that physical reading.

findings: Privacy item tested general mass reference without a substantial B2 distinction.
audit.microSkill: Zero article in the idiomatic phrase by design
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a fixed article-free phrase in a meaningful contrast.
audit.levelReason: The learner must distinguish an idiomatic abstract use from ordinary noun reference.
audit.similarityNote: Only phrase expressing intentionality.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the definite noun phrase.
items.taskText: "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
options: One particular car whose owner has been identified
Electric cars as a technological category
The first electric car manufactured in the city
Only electric cars owned by city planners
items.answer: Electric cars as a technological category
items.explanation: A definite singular can represent a class or invention. In this general discussion, "the electric car" means the technology or vehicle type, not one physical car.

rationales.One particular car whose owner has been: No owner or individual vehicle is established; the broad planning context supports a category reading.
rationales.Electric cars as a technological categor: The definite singular represents the vehicle type in a general claim about change.
rationales.The first electric car manufactured in t: "The" does not add a first-in-history meaning or a manufacturing location.
rationales.Only electric cars owned by city planner: The sentence concerns city planning, not ownership by the people doing it.

findings: Original option-that sentence was only an-before-vowel despite a following clause.
audit.microSkill: Generic definite singular for a technological category
audit.pedagogicalValue: Counters the rule that the always points to one previously mentioned object.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a category-level statement in a public-policy context suits B2 reading.
audit.similarityNote: Generic invention reference rather than an individual service or named place.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article change.
items.taskText: Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
options: It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
It says her practical knowledge is greater than that of other nurses
It identifies an event that the listener has already heard about
It says the event was unusual or dangerous
items.answer: It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
