rationales.The indefinite article introduces a seco: An expected phenomenon is being characterised more precisely after the encounter. The article does not itself establish two separate episodes.
rationales.The article identifies resistance as sha: A detailed description need not create definite shared reference. Here a presents the kind or manifestation encountered.
rationales.The resistance is presented as a particu: The modifier specifies what this opposition was like and where it came from, licensing a characterised indefinite use.
rationales.The article turns the cause into a defin: The phrase characterises this manifestation, not resistance in general. Other resistance need not arise from broken promises.

findings: Original alternative-reading item tested only an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite article with a characterised manifestation of an abstract noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a literary use without teaching that every modified abstract noun needs a.
audit.levelReason: Requires sensitivity to rhetorical recategorisation in connected prose.
audit.similarityNote: Characterised social opposition differs from an individual reservation or negotiated arrangement.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation that accounts for the narrator's correction.
items.taskText: 'The chair took a silence for the silence of agreement; in fact, nobody had understood the proposal.' Why can the writer use 'the silence of agreement' without saying that the group agreed?
options: The definite phrase names the interpretation the chair imposed, rather than one the narrator endorses
The definite phrase establishes agreement as a fact, while the ending questions only its wisdom
The definite phrase identifies an earlier agreement, so the ending refers to a different proposal
The definite phrase specifies a duration of silence, leaving the group's attitude outside its meaning
items.answer: The definite phrase names the interpretation the chair imposed, rather than one the narrator endorses
items.explanation: 'Took X for Y' can report a mistaken interpretation. A silence introduces the pause; the silence of agreement describes what the chair wrongly thought it represented. The definite phrase belongs inside that attributed interpretation, which the narrator then corrects.

rationales.The definite phrase names the interpreta: The article identifies a kind of meaningful silence within the chair's mistaken reading of events.
rationales.The definite phrase establishes agreemen: The phrase is within 'took ... for', not an independent assertion of agreement. The ending explains why the chair's interpretation was mistaken.
rationales.The definite phrase identifies an earlie: No earlier agreement or second proposal is introduced. The contrast concerns two interpretations of the same pause.
rationales.The definite phrase specifies a duration: 'Of agreement' attributes communicative significance to the silence; it does not measure how long the pause lasted.

findings: Original treats silence as evidence allowed a particular-silence reading and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Definite description inside an attributed but mistaken interpretation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that an identifiable description within a reported viewpoint is not automatically the narrator's factual commitment.
audit.levelReason: Requires tracking article reference through an attribution of belief and a subsequent correction.
audit.similarityNote: A mistaken viewpoint, distinct from conditional reference and countable emotional qualities.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the modified indefinite noun phrase.
items.taskText: "A novel of this kind rewards a patient reader." The critic is making a general claim about a genre, rather than reviewing one identified book. Why is "a novel of this kind" appropriate?
options: It introduces one particular novel whose title the critic has chosen to withhold
It presents a representative member of the genre without identifying an individual book
It implies that only one novel belongs to the kind being discussed
It identifies a book through a modifier, so a and the have identical force here
items.answer: It presents a representative member of the genre without identifying an individual book
items.explanation: An indefinite singular can support a generalisation by representing a member of a class. The modifier "of this kind" restricts the class; it does not by itself turn the phrase into definite reference to an individual book.

rationales.It introduces one particular novel whose: That is one possible use of an indefinite phrase elsewhere, but the stated genre-level claim establishes a representative reading here.
rationales.It presents a representative member of t: This preserves the generalisation while treating the novel as a representative class member.
rationales.It implies that only one novel belongs t: An indefinite singular used generically does not limit the class to one member.
rationales.It identifies a book through a modifier,: A modifier can restrict a class without identifying a unique individual. The two articles do not become interchangeable merely because a modifier follows.

findings: Original only-reading item forced the through a repeated elementary frame.
audit.microSkill: Representative generic indefinite with a postmodified singular noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches that postmodification and specificity are separate decisions.
audit.levelReason: Distinguishes generic, specific-indefinite, and definite readings of a modified noun phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Representative generic reference in literary criticism, distinct from known individuals and hypothetical existence.

items.setupText: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the article's effect.
items.taskText: "It was not merely an inconvenience; it was the inconvenience that finally made her leave." What does the second article contribute?
options: It turns every inconvenience she had suffered into a single event
It identifies this inconvenience by its decisive consequence
It proves that she had never suffered an inconvenience before
It changes inconvenience from an event into an uncountable emotional state
items.answer: It identifies this inconvenience by its decisive consequence
items.explanation: "An inconvenience" first classifies the event. "The inconvenience that finally made her leave" identifies it through a distinguishing consequence. The definite article does not deny the existence of other inconveniences.

rationales.It turns every inconvenience she had suf: The definite phrase selects the decisive event; it does not merge multiple events.
rationales.It identifies this inconvenience by its: The following clause specifies what makes this event identifiable in the narrative.
rationales.It proves that she had never suffered an: Other inconveniences may have occurred. "Finally" even makes a sequence of problems plausible.
rationales.It changes inconvenience from an event i: Both occurrences remain countable event uses; the change concerns reference, not noun class.

findings: Original public-meaning item repeated a weak the-plus-postmodifier cloze.
audit.microSkill: Definiteness established by a distinguishing consequence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates identification from claims of absolute uniqueness.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting narrative emphasis and the restrictive clause without overclaiming what the implies.
audit.similarityNote: Retrospective identification by outcome rather than previous naming or shared setting.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation that the article contrast supports.
items.taskText: "She spoke with authority, though she was not an authority on the period." What is contrasted?
options: Permission to speak versus ownership of the historical records
A commanding manner versus the status of a recognised specialist
An official position versus an unofficial position within the same organisation
Confidence about the dates versus uncertainty about the people
items.answer: A commanding manner versus the status of a recognised specialist
items.explanation: Article-free "authority" describes the manner or force of her speech. "An authority on" is a countable expression for a recognised expert in a subject.

rationales.Permission to speak versus ownership of: Authority can mean permission elsewhere, but "spoke with authority" naturally describes manner; ownership is not asserted.
rationales.A commanding manner versus the status of: This preserves the manner noun in the first clause and the person-denoting noun phrase in the second.
rationales.An official position versus an unofficia: No organisation or institutional post is identified. "An authority on" names expertise, not an employment category.
rationales.Confidence about the dates versus uncert: The wording does not divide her knowledge into dates and people.

findings: Original equivocal-pattern question was elementary a/an with inflated vocabulary.
audit.microSkill: Mass quality versus countable expert in authority
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects article choice to a change in noun sense and grammatical reference.
audit.levelReason: Interprets an idiomatic contrast between forceful presentation and subject expertise.
audit.similarityNote: A manner-to-person sense contrast, different from expert prominence.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation licensed by the phrase.
items.taskText: "The correspondence reveals the Paris of her youth rather than the city the tourist brochures describe." What does "the Paris of her youth" identify?
options: A different city formally named Paris during her youth
The city as experienced or represented in a particular period of her life
An unidentified city sharing some Parisian characteristics
A set of letters whose published title is Paris of Her Youth
items.answer: The city as experienced or represented in a particular period of her life
items.explanation: The definite article and modifier select a temporally and personally characterised version of a place. Paris remains the same city; the phrase directs attention to the Paris represented by her youthful experience.

rationales.A different city formally named Paris du: The phrase need not refer to another municipality or a name change; it frames the familiar city through a period of experience.
rationales.The city as experienced or represented i: This captures how the modifier licenses a definite, characterised use of the proper name.
rationales.An unidentified city sharing some Parisi: That would resemble a metaphorical "a Paris" reading, not the identified version of the city described here.
rationales.A set of letters whose published title i: The words identify what the correspondence reveals, not a title assigned to the letters.

findings: Original guidance-on-data-retention item permitted the guidance and had no specific feedback.
audit.microSkill: Definite article with a temporally characterised place name
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains an exception to the simplistic rule that city names never take the.
audit.levelReason: The interpretation combines proper-name reference, narrative perspective, and temporal characterisation.
audit.similarityNote: Place-and-period framing contrasts with the indefinite portrayal of Shakespeare.

items.setupText: Choose the inference warranted by the indefinite phrase.
items.taskText: "If there is a flaw in the proof, the flaw will lie in the induction step." Which reading is accurate?
options: The writer asserts that the proof contains exactly one flaw
The writer has identified a flaw but is withholding its location
The second phrase refers back to a flaw under the stated condition, without asserting that one exists
The writer excludes flaws in other proofs because the noun is definite
items.answer: The second phrase refers back to a flaw under the stated condition, without asserting that one exists
items.explanation: "A flaw" is introduced inside an if-condition. "The flaw" can refer back inside that hypothetical reasoning without committing the writer to the existence of a flaw.

rationales.The writer asserts that the proof contai: The conditional introduction does not assert existence, much less an exact count of actual flaws.
rationales.The writer has identified a flaw but is: The writer explicitly proposes a location while leaving existence conditional.
rationales.The second phrase refers back to a flaw: This keeps the definite reference within the hypothetical situation introduced by if.
rationales.The writer excludes flaws in other proof: The article identifies the locally introduced possibility; it says nothing about other proofs.

findings: Original procedural-defect item reduced C2 articles to a before a consonant.
audit.microSkill: Anaphoric definiteness without an assertion of existence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents treating every definite noun phrase as an unconditional existence claim.
audit.levelReason: Requires reasoning about reference within conditional scope.
audit.similarityNote: Hypothetical existence differs from the repeated appointment situations in item 461.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article phrase.
items.taskText: "For all his objections, he remained a believer in the project, if not the believer his colleagues had hoped for." What does the final phrase imply?
options: His colleagues had envisaged a kind of supporter whose commitment he did not fully display
His colleagues wanted another supporter to replace him because they considered him an opponent
His colleagues recognised him as their leading supporter but had not expected his objections
His colleagues doubted his private support because his public commitment exceeded their expectations
items.answer: His colleagues had envisaged a kind of supporter whose commitment he did not fully display
items.explanation: "A believer" grants membership in the category of supporters. "The believer his colleagues had hoped for" refers to their envisaged kind of committed supporter. The contrast qualifies his support without cancelling it.

rationales.His colleagues had envisaged a kind of s: The indefinite phrase grants that he supports the project; the definite description measures him against their unrealised expectation.
rationales.His colleagues wanted another supporter: 'He remained a believer' affirms support. The contrast concerns the kind of supporter he was, not a stated plan to replace an opponent.
rationales.His colleagues recognised him as their l: The relative clause identifies an envisaged supporter, not an established leading figure. 'If not' withholds the hoped-for characterisation.
rationales.His colleagues doubted his private suppo: The sentence neither divides public from private belief nor says he exceeded their expectations; he falls short of the hoped-for characterisation.

findings: Original only-defect item repeated a mechanically forced definite answer.
audit.microSkill: Definite phrase identifying an envisaged standard of a person
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a restrictive clause can identify an expected role without introducing a second person.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting concession, degree of commitment, and an intensional definite description.
audit.similarityNote: An expected persona differs from recognised pre-eminence in the expert contrast.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation that fits both examples.
items.taskText: Compare "She went to court to challenge the decision" and "She went to the court to photograph its entrance". What is the principal effect of the article?
options: The first frames participation in proceedings; the second identifies a place in this context
The bare phrase identifies any court, while the definite phrase always identifies a building

items.answer: The first frames participation in proceedings; the second identifies a place in this context
items.explanation: "Go to court" conventionally means engaging with legal proceedings. "Go to the court" can identify a particular institution or location; photographing its entrance makes the physical-place reading salient. The contrast is contextual, not a rule that the always means a building.

rationales.The first frames participation in procee: The bare institutional expression and the stated photographic purpose together support this qualified distinction.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation of the changed noun phrase.
items.taskText: A reviewer writes "The chapter offers history, not nostalgia". Another writes "The chapter offers a history, not a memoir". What change accompanies the added articles?
options: Both reviewers describe a single historical account; only the second says whether it is personal
The first contrasts approaches to the past; the second classifies an account by genre
The first judges the account's accuracy; the second establishes that the chapter is a complete book
Both contrast genres; the added articles identify particular accounts already familiar to the reader
items.answer: The first contrasts approaches to the past; the second classifies an account by genre
items.explanation: Article-free "history" and "nostalgia" contrast ways of treating the past. "A history" and "a memoir" count kinds of account. Neither article choice establishes accuracy or whether the account is fictional.

rationales.Both reviewers describe a single histori: The first bare-noun contrast need not count a single account: a chapter can offer historical treatment rather than nostalgic treatment without constituting an individual history.
rationales.The first contrasts approaches to the pa: Bare nouns describe modes of treatment; a history and a memoir package accounts as countable genre instances.
rationales.The first judges the account's accuracy;: The first may praise its approach without guaranteeing accuracy. A chapter can offer a history without being a complete book.
rationales.Both contrast genres; the added articles: The indefinite articles classify accounts without presenting them as already familiar. The first contrast is between historical and nostalgic treatment.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects article use to whether a noun denotes a mode of treatment or an individual account.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting evaluative critical prose and keeping genre classification separate from truth claims.
audit.similarityNote: Textual genre contrast, distinct from countable agreements and acts of silence.

items.setupText: Choose the wording that keeps the writer's intended reference.
items.taskText: An anthropologist means the human capacity for language as a whole, rather than any one named language or a community's particular usage. Which phrase makes that distinction clearest?
options: the emergence of a language
the emergence of the language
the emergence of language
the emergence of one language
items.answer: the emergence of language
items.explanation: Article-free "language" can denote the human capacity or phenomenon. "A language" counts an individual linguistic system, while "the language" normally identifies a particular system or usage. The stated intention selects the uncountable general reading.

rationales.the emergence of a language: The indefinite article presents one linguistic system, which is narrower than the capacity meant here.
rationales.the emergence of the language: The definite phrase invites identification of a particular language or usage from context; the prompt deliberately excludes that reference.
rationales.the emergence of language: With no article before "language", the phrase supports the intended capacity-level meaning.
rationales.the emergence of one language: "One" explicitly counts a single language and therefore changes the scope of the claim.

findings: Original only-methodology item ended another repeated definite-article frame.
audit.microSkill: Article choice distinguishing a human capacity from an individual system
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes learners attend to the scope of abstract reference when editing scholarly prose.
audit.levelReason: The language is accessible but the referential distinction affects the exact scope of an academic claim.
audit.similarityNote: Capacity-versus-system reference closes the set with a different count/mass distinction.
